Dissolved
dĭ-zōlvd'
v. (loosed apart, broken up; used of cities, of the earth, and of the host of heaven)
Latin dissolvere, to loosen apart, from dis-, asunder, and solvere, to loose. What is dissolved is not merely damaged; the bonds that held it together are undone.

Biblical Definition

Scripture reserves this word for the undoing of things men assume are permanent. A city: “Howl, O gate; cry, O city; thou, whole Palestina, art dissolved” (Isa 14:31). A palace: “The gates of the rivers shall be opened, and the palace shall be dissolved” (Nah 2:6). The earth itself: “The earth is utterly broken down, the earth is clean dissolved, the earth is moved exceedingly” (Isa 24:19). Even the sky: “And all the host of heaven shall be dissolved, and the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll” (Isa 34:4). Against this the psalmist hears God speak in the first person: “The earth and all the inhabitants thereof are dissolved: I bear up the pillars of it. Selah” (Psa 75:3). The dissolution is real and the pillars are borne up by a hand; both clauses stand in one verse. Peter draws the practical conclusion and it is not speculation about dates but a question about character: “Seeing then that all these things shall be dissolved, what manner of persons ought ye to be in all holy conversation and godliness” (2Pe 3:11).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to dissolve as to melt, to liquefy; to break, to disunite, to loosen the parts of a thing; and to break up an assembly or dissolve a body politic.

expand to see more

DISSOLVE, v.t. dizzolv'. [L. dissolvo; dis and solvo, to loose.] To melt; to liquefy; to convert from a solid or fixed state to a fluid state.

2. To disunite; to break; to separate.

3. To loose; to disunite; as, to dissolve a league or a friendship.

All these things shall be dissolved. 2 Pet. iii.

Key Scripture

Isa 24:19 — "The earth is utterly broken down, the earth is clean dissolved, the earth is moved exceedingly."

Isa 34:4 — "And all the host of heaven shall be dissolved, and the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll: and all their host shall fall down, as the leaf falleth off from the vine, and as a falling fig from the fig tree."

Psa 75:3 — "The earth and all the inhabitants thereof are dissolved: I bear up the pillars of it. Selah."

2Pe 3:11 — "Seeing then that all these things shall be dissolved, what manner of persons ought ye to be in all holy conversation and godliness,"

Modern Corruption

The dissolution of all things is treated either as poetry that means nothing or as a calendar to be decoded, while Peter draws from it one plain question about how a man lives.

expand to see more

Two habits keep the church from hearing 2 Peter 3. The first empties the language: the passage is called apocalyptic imagery, a way of speaking about upheaval in general, and the plain assertion that the elements shall melt with fervent heat is quietly filed as a figure. The apostle's own argument forbids it — he grounds the coming dissolution in a past event of the same kind, the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished, and he says the scoffers of the last days will be men who are willingly ignorant of that flood. Deny the first judgment and the second becomes unimaginable, which is exactly the mechanism he describes. The second habit is the mirror image: the passage becomes a code, matched against current events, and a generation is fed dates that pass. Peter draws no date from it at all. From all these things shall be dissolved he draws one question, and it concerns conduct.

Psalm 75:3 keeps the doctrine from becoming terror. In one verse the earth and all its inhabitants are dissolved, and God says I bear up the pillars of it. Nothing dissolves outside His hand, and the same hand that will one day fold the heavens as a scroll is holding the floor up under the reader this morning. That is why the Christian doctrine of the last things is not a doctrine of panic, and why the practical counsel that flows from it is holy conversation and godliness rather than hoarding or withdrawal. A man who knows the house is coming down invests in what will not, and Peter says exactly what that is in the following verse: we, according to his promise, look for new heavens and a new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mug (H4127), to melt or dissolve; parar (H6565), to break apart; Greek luo (G3089), to loose, used by Peter of the dissolving of all things.

expand to see more

Hebrew mug (H4127) — to melt, to dissolve; the earth and all the inhabitants thereof are dissolved; Psalm 75:3.

Hebrew parar (H6565) — to break, to make void; the earth is clean dissolved; Isaiah 24:19.

Hebrew maqaq (H4743) — to pine away, to melt; all the host of heaven shall be dissolved; Isaiah 34:4.

Greek luo (G3089) — to loose, to break up; all these things shall be dissolved; 2 Peter 3:11.

Greek stoicheion (G4747) — an element, a first principle; the elements that shall melt with fervent heat; 2 Peter 3:10.

Usage

"“The earth is clean dissolved” — the undoing of what men assume is permanent."

"“I bear up the pillars of it” — in the same verse as the dissolving."

"“What manner of persons ought ye to be” — the only inference Peter draws."
